name: financial_accounting_set3_p1
label: Financial Accounting: set 3 (control, departmental, branch, incomplete records, partnerships)

papers.title: Control Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on control accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The credit sales figure in a sales ledger control account is taken from the
questions.explanation:
Control accounts are written up from totals in the books of original entry.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cash book: The cash book gives receipts, not credit sales.
- purchases day book: That gives credit purchases.
- returns inwards book: That gives returns inwards.

questions.stem: Which item appears on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
questions.explanation:
Discount allowed reduces what customers owe, so it is credited.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- credit sales: Credit sales are a debit.
- dishonoured cheques: Dishonoured cheques are a debit: the customer owes again.
- discount received: Discount received belongs in the purchases ledger control account.

questions.stem: Debits in a sales ledger control account total NLe 166,800 and credits before the balance total NLe 107,800. The closing balance is
questions.explanation:
166,800 − 107,800 = 59,000, a debit balance: total owed by customers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a credit balance of NLe 59,000: The debit side is larger.
- a debit balance of NLe 274,600: The sides have been added.
- a debit balance of NLe 107,800: That is the credit total.

questions.stem: A set-off of NLe 2,000 between the sales and purchases ledgers is recorded in the control accounts by
questions.explanation:
The amount owed to the supplier (credit balance) falls with a debit; the amount owed by the customer (debit balance) falls with a credit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debiting sales ledger control and crediting purchases ledger control: That reverses the entry.
- debiting both control accounts: A set-off reduces both balances: one debit and one credit.
- crediting both control accounts: A set-off reduces both balances: one debit and one credit.

options.label: A
options.content: debiting sales ledger control and crediting purchases ledger control

options.label: D
options.content: debiting purchases ledger control and crediting sales ledger control

questions.stem: Which item is NOT entered in a sales ledger control account?
questions.explanation:
Cash sales never pass through a customer's personal account.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- returns inwards: Returns inwards reduce customers' balances.
- bad debts written off: Bad debts reduce customers' balances.
- cash received from customers: Receipts reduce customers' balances.

papers.title: Departmental Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on departmental accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The most suitable basis for apportioning rent between departments is
questions.explanation:
Rent is paid for space, so floor area is the fairest basis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sales: Sales suit costs such as advertising.
- number of employees: Staff numbers suit canteen costs.
- value of equipment: Equipment value suits depreciation and insurance of equipment.

questions.stem: Rent of NLe 36,000 is shared by floor area between departments occupying 300, 200 and 100 square metres. The largest department bears
questions.explanation:
300 ÷ 600 × 36,000 = 18,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 12,000: That is the share of the 200 square-metre department.
- NLe 12,000 each: The rent is shared by area, not equally.
- NLe 6,000: That is the share of the smallest department.

questions.stem: Advertising of NLe 10,000 is apportioned on sales of NLe 120,000 and NLe 180,000. The first department bears
questions.explanation:
Sales ratio 120 : 180 = 2 : 3; 2/5 × 10,000 = 4,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 6,000: That is the second department's share.
- NLe 5,000: The cost is shared by sales, not equally.
- NLe 1,200: That is not the correct proportion.

questions.stem: Charging the wages of a department's own sales staff wholly to that department is called
questions.explanation:
Direct expenses are allocated to the department that caused them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- apportionment: Apportionment shares a cost between departments.
- absorption: That is a costing term for charging overheads to products.
- appropriation: Appropriation shares profit, as in partnerships.

questions.stem: Department X had sales of NLe 120,000 and gross profit of NLe 53,000. Its gross profit margin is about
questions.explanation:
53,000 ÷ 120,000 × 100% ≈ 44.2%.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 53.0%: The margin divides gross profit by sales, not by 100,000.
- 79.1%: That divides gross profit by cost of sales.
- 226.4%: That divides sales by gross profit.

papers.title: Branch Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on branch accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A branch that receives its goods from head office and sends all its cash to head office is
questions.explanation:
Head office supplies and controls a dependent branch and keeps its accounts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an independent branch: An independent branch keeps its own books.
- a subsidiary company: A subsidiary is a separate company.
- a joint venture: A joint venture is a temporary partnership.

questions.stem: In a branch account kept by head office, goods sent to the branch at cost are
questions.explanation:
Everything head office sends or pays for the branch is debited to the branch account.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- credited to the branch account: Goods sent increase what the branch is accountable for.
- debited to sales: Goods sent to a branch are not sales.
- credited to cash: No cash is paid.

questions.stem: Opening branch receivables NLe 3,000; cash from receivables NLe 25,000; closing receivables NLe 5,000. Branch credit sales are
questions.explanation:
25,000 + 5,000 − 3,000 = 27,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 23,000: Closing receivables must be added and opening deducted.
- NLe 33,000: Opening receivables must be deducted, not added.
- NLe 25,000: That is only the cash collected.

questions.stem: Goods are sent to a branch at cost plus 25%. The loading is what fraction of the selling price?
questions.explanation:
Cost 100, selling price 125; loading 25 ÷ 125 = 1/5.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- one-quarter: 25% is the mark-up on cost, not on selling price.
- one-third: That would be a 50% mark-up.
- one-half: That would be a 100% mark-up.

questions.stem: A difference on the branch stock account kept at selling price shows
questions.explanation:
At selling price, opening stock plus goods sent should equal sales plus closing stock; any difference is a loss or surplus.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the branch gross profit: Gross profit is found in the branch adjustment account.
- the branch's expenses: Expenses are recorded separately.
- the value of goods returned to head office: Returns are recorded as entries, not as the balancing difference.

options.label: C
options.content: a shortage or surplus of goods or cash at the branch

options.label: D
options.content: the value of goods returned to head office

papers.title: Single Entry and Incomplete Records: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on single entry and incomplete records, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A statement of affairs is used to find a business's
questions.explanation:
Capital = assets − liabilities, listed in the statement of affairs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gross profit for the year: Gross profit needs a trading account.
- cash received during the year: That comes from cash records.
- credit sales for the year: Credit sales come from a total receivables account.

questions.stem: Opening capital NLe 36,000; closing capital NLe 40,000; drawings NLe 14,000; capital introduced NLe 3,000. Profit is
questions.explanation:
40,000 − 36,000 + 14,000 − 3,000 = 15,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 4,000: Drawings must be added and capital introduced deducted.
- NLe 21,000: Capital introduced must be deducted, not added.
- NLe 18,000: Capital introduced has not been deducted.

questions.stem: Opening receivables NLe 5,000; closing NLe 7,000; cash received NLe 60,000; discount allowed NLe 1,000. Credit sales are
questions.explanation:
60,000 + 1,000 + 7,000 − 5,000 = 63,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 59,000: Discount allowed and closing receivables must be added.
- NLe 73,000: Opening receivables must be deducted, not added.
- NLe 61,000: Closing receivables must be added and opening deducted.

questions.stem: A mark-up of 25% is equal to a margin of
questions.explanation:
Cost 100, sales 125; margin = 25 ÷ 125 = 20%.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 25%: Margin is based on sales, so it is smaller than the mark-up.
- 33⅓%: That is the margin for a 50% mark-up.
- 75%: Cost is 80% of sales, so the gross profit margin is 20%, not 75%.

questions.stem: Opening inventory NLe 15,000; purchases NLe 70,000; sales NLe 90,000 at a mark-up of 25%. Goods worth NLe 4,000 at cost were saved from a fire. Inventory lost is
questions.explanation:
Cost of sales = 90,000 × 100/125 = 72,000; expected inventory = 15,000 + 70,000 − 72,000 = 13,000; lost = 13,000 − 4,000 = 9,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 13,000: The goods saved must be deducted.
- NLe 5,000: Cost of sales is 72,000, not 67,500.
- NLe 17,000: The goods saved must be deducted, not added.

papers.title: Joint Venture and Consignment Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on joint venture and consignment accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A joint venture differs from a partnership because a joint venture
questions.explanation:
A joint venture ends when its project is complete; a partnership is a continuing business.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- has unlimited liability: Ordinary partners also have unlimited liability.
- shares profits between members: Partnerships also share profits.
- must have more than twenty members: There is no such rule.

options.label: A
options.content: is temporary and formed for a specific project

options.label: D
options.content: must have more than twenty members

questions.stem: Costs of a joint venture total NLe 23,000 and sales NLe 30,000. Profit is shared equally. Each co-venturer's share is
questions.explanation:
Profit = 30,000 − 23,000 = 7,000; each share = 3,500.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 7,000: That is the total profit.
- NLe 15,000: That is half the sales.
- NLe 11,500: That is half the costs.

questions.stem: The statement sent by a consignee to the consignor showing sales, expenses and commission is the
questions.explanation:
The account sales reports the results of the consignment and the balance due.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pro-forma invoice: The pro-forma invoice is sent by the consignor with the goods.
- credit note: A credit note records returns or overcharges.
- statement of affairs: A statement of affairs is used with incomplete records.

questions.stem: Commission paid to a consignee for bearing the risk of bad debts is called
questions.explanation:
Del credere commission compensates the consignee for guaranteeing credit sales.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ordinary commission: Ordinary commission is for selling the goods.
- overriding commission: Overriding commission rewards extra effort or special sales.
- trade discount: Trade discount is a reduction in list price.

questions.stem: 100 bags costing NLe 600 each are consigned, with freight of NLe 3,000. 20 bags remain unsold. Their value is
questions.explanation:
20 × 600 + 20/100 × 3,000 = 12,000 + 600 = 12,600.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 12,000: A share of the freight must be added.
- NLe 15,000: Only 20% of the freight belongs to the unsold bags.
- NLe 18,000: That values the bags at selling price.

papers.title: Bills of Exchange: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on bills of exchange, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The person who draws a bill of exchange is usually the
questions.explanation:
The creditor (seller) draws the bill on the debtor (buyer).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debtor: The debtor is the drawee who accepts the bill.
- bank: A bank may discount a bill but does not usually draw it.
- auditor: Auditors are not parties to a bill.

questions.stem: A bill for NLe 10,000 with two months to run is discounted at 12% a year. The proceeds are
questions.explanation:
Discount = 10,000 × 12% × 2/12 = 200; proceeds = 9,800.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 8,800: That uses the full annual rate instead of two months.
- NLe 9,700: That uses three months instead of two.
- NLe 10,200: Discount is deducted, not added.

questions.stem: When a customer accepts a bill, the drawer records
questions.explanation:
The debt moves from the customer's account to the bills receivable account.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit the customer, credit bills receivable: That reverses the entry.
- debit bills payable, credit the customer: Bills payable are recorded by the acceptor.
- debit bank, credit bills receivable: That records payment of the bill.

options.label: A
options.content: debit the customer, credit bills receivable

options.label: B
options.content: debit bills payable, credit the customer

options.label: D
options.content: debit bills receivable, credit the customer

questions.stem: In the acceptor's books, bills payable are
questions.explanation:
The acceptor must pay the bill on the due date: a short-term liability.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a current asset: Bills receivable are a current asset.
- an expense: Bills payable are amounts owed.
- part of capital: They are owed to a supplier, not the owner.

questions.stem: A bill that the drawer has discounted is dishonoured on the due date. The drawer credits
questions.explanation:
The bank reclaims the money, so the drawer credits the bank and debits the customer.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- bills receivable: Bills receivable was already cleared when the bill was discounted.
- the customer: The customer is debited, because they owe again.
- sales: No sale is reversed.

papers.title: Non-Profit Organisation Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on non-profit organisation accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The capital of a club is called the
questions.explanation:
The accumulated fund equals the club's assets minus its liabilities.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- share capital: Share capital is the capital of a company.
- general reserve: A general reserve is a company reserve.
- current account: Current accounts belong to partners.

questions.stem: The balance of a receipts and payments account represents
questions.explanation:
A receipts and payments account summarises the cash book.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the surplus for the year: The surplus comes from the income and expenditure account.
- the accumulated fund: The accumulated fund is assets minus liabilities.
- subscriptions in arrears: Arrears are not shown in a receipts and payments account.

options.label: D
options.content: cash in hand and at bank

questions.stem: Subscriptions received NLe 18,000; opening arrears NLe 1,000; opening in advance NLe 500; closing arrears NLe 1,500; closing in advance NLe 800. Subscription income is
questions.explanation:
18,000 − 1,000 + 500 + 1,500 − 800 = 18,200.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 18,000: That is cash received, not income for the year.
- NLe 17,800: The adjustments have been applied in the wrong direction.
- NLe 21,800: All the adjustments have been added.

questions.stem: An excess of income over expenditure in a club's accounts is called a
questions.explanation:
The income and expenditure account ends with a surplus or a deficit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- net profit: Clubs do not aim to make profit; the term is surplus.
- deficit: A deficit is an excess of expenditure over income.
- gross profit: Gross profit belongs to trading activities.

questions.stem: New sports equipment bought by a club is shown in the income and expenditure account as
questions.explanation:
The equipment goes to the statement of financial position; only depreciation is charged as expenditure.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its full cost: Equipment is a capital item.
- income: It is an asset, not income.
- nothing at all: Its depreciation is charged.

papers.title: Partnership Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on partnership accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the absence of a partnership agreement, profits are shared
questions.explanation:
The usual legal rule is equal sharing of profits and losses.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in the ratio of capitals: Without agreement, capital does not decide shares.
- in the ratio of hours worked: Hours worked do not decide shares.
- according to the oldest partner: No such rule exists.

options.label: B
options.content: in the ratio of hours worked

questions.stem: Without an agreement, interest on a partner's loan to the firm is allowed at
questions.explanation:
The legal rule allows 5% a year on partners' loans beyond capital.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10% a year: The usual legal rate is 5%.
- the bank's lending rate: A fixed legal rate applies.
- nothing: Interest on partners' loans is allowed.

questions.stem: Net profit NLe 50,000; interest on drawings NLe 1,000; partner's salary NLe 8,000; interest on capital NLe 10,000. The residual profit is
questions.explanation:
50,000 + 1,000 − 8,000 − 10,000 = 33,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 31,000: Interest on drawings must be added.
- NLe 50,000: Salary and interest on capital must be deducted.
- NLe 69,000: Salary and interest are deductions, not additions.

questions.stem: A partner's salary is shown in the
questions.explanation:
Salaries and interest on capital share out profit among partners.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- income statement as an expense: It is an appropriation of profit, not an expense.
- statement of financial position as a liability: It is credited to the current account first.
- trading account: The trading account finds gross profit.

options.label: B
options.content: statement of financial position as a liability

questions.stem: Average profits are NLe 40,000 and goodwill is two years' purchase. Goodwill is
questions.explanation:
40,000 × 2 = 80,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 20,000: Goodwill is profit multiplied, not divided, by years.
- NLe 40,000: That is one year's profit.
- NLe 120,000: That is three years' purchase.
